title: Govt. opens Rs. 2 t pipeline to private sector, shuts door on unsolicited deals | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:55
-     - 12

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma - Pic by Upul Abayasekara

By Charumini de Silva

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma yesterday said the private sector could tap an estimated Rs. 2 trillion in public investment opportunities in 2027, but through transparent and competitive procurement rather than unsolicited proposals. This comes as the Government moves to legislate a level playing field between State-owned Enterprises (SOEs) and private businesses.

Delivering the keynote address at the 16th edition of the Daily FT-Colombo University MBA Alumni Association Post-Budget Forum, he said Budget 2027 was designed to consolidate the macroeconomic stabilisation achieved over the past two years, whilst shifting the focus towards production, competitiveness, technology and broader economic participation.

Dr. Suriyapperuma stressed that the Government’s development agenda could not be delivered by the State alone, calling for businesses, professionals, consultants and human resource specialists to contribute their expertise and capacity to execute an expanding pipeline of public investment projects.

“The challenge is no longer simply to formulate ambitious plans, but to build the national capacity to implement them, withstand external shocks and create a competitive economy in which both public and private enterprises could thrive,” he said.

Dr. Suriyapperuma said the Rs. 2 trillion allocation for 2027 would create substantial opportunities across highways, roads, railways, ports, airports, sports infrastructure and other development projects, whilst providing a pathway for businesses to expand beyond the 22 million domestic market.

He outlined implementation capacity, financing capacity and resilience against external shocks as three critical tests for the country’s ability to deliver on its ambitions. “These could translate Budget allocations into tangible economic outcomes amid geopolitical uncertainty, climate-related disasters and other risks beyond our control.”

The Treasury Secretary asserted that the Government has demonstrated its capacity and ability to stabilise the economy through improved fiscal discipline, stronger foreign reserves and sovereign rating, while successfully progressing through the IMF-supported program, with its final review expected in March 2027.

“This progress should help restore investor confidence, particularly among long-term domestic and foreign investors who had become cautious following the economic crisis,” he said, adding that the Government’s commitment to the rule of law, equal treatment and zero tolerance for corruption was essential to creating a more predictable investment environment.

He said a key distinction in the new investment approach was the rejection of unsolicited proposals and projects that lacked adequate feasibility assessment in favour of transparent and competitive procurement.

Citing the renewable energy sector as an example, he said wind and BESS projects awarded through an open process had demonstrated the benefits of competition and procurement reforms. Dr. Suriyapperuma pointed out that those were not evidence of the Government turning away investment, but of its determination to secure better value for citizens and taxpayers, whilst strengthening the competitiveness of the economy.

“Budget 2027 rests on seven broad objectives and six strategic pillars, supported by around 40 implementation measures. These include: macroeconomic stability, a production-oriented economy, technology, human capital development, regional economic integration, energy security and climate resilience alongside improvements to the Government’s delivery mechanism,” he outlined.

He said a key priority is to reposition Sri Lanka as a production economy to compete for global markets, which would require targeted investment in manufacturing and services, technological advancement, research and development, skills and productivity.

Dr. Suriyapperuma also stressed the need to connect rural and regional economies more effectively with national economic activity through improved infrastructure, access to finance, digital tools and business advisory services.

Highlighting the Government’s efforts to improve public sector efficiency, he cited the implementation of the digital VAT refund mechanism as an example of how long-standing administrative bottlenecks could be addressed through engagement with business and institutional reform.

In addition, he highlighted the paperless Customs initiative introduced on 1 October and the National Single Window (NSW) platform, which went live in a limited implementation phase on 5 November. “The NSW is being rolled out in phases, beginning with exports, followed by imports and transhipment. Tea and coconut have been selected for the first phase covering over 120 HS codes, with initial shipments successfully processed via the digital system. These initiatives are intended to reduce administrative delays, improve transparency and allow businesses to concentrate on operations, rather than navigating multiple agencies for approvals and clearances,” he explained.

The Treasury Secretary said the SME sector will receive a larger financing allocation in 2027, with Rs. 174 billion earmarked compared to Rs. 97 billion in the 2026 Budget.

Noting that the Government has achieved full commitments under most of the 2026 lending initiatives by 30 September, he said an additional Rs. 7 billion allocation was approved by the Cabinet of Ministers for disbursement during November and December.

He attributed the progress to closer monitoring by the Treasury through monthly discussions with commercial banks and relevant State institutions, whilst adding that in the 2027 package, the commercial banks will have a key role in identifying and financing eligible enterprises through their networks.

In addition, Dr. Suriyapperuma said the Government’s delivery record had attracted further support from a multilateral development partner, which had pledged additional financing to expand the collateral-free lending initiative.

In fisheries, he cited a financing facility enabling businesses to borrow up to Rs. 500 million at an interest rate of 5% to acquire a single fishing vessel, underscoring the Government’s ambition to develop a competitive deep-sea fishing fleet.

He said the Government is also pursuing reforms to facilitate public-private partnerships (PPPs), with the PPP Bill gazetted, aiming to provide a clearer framework for private sector participation in public projects.

Dr. Suriyapperuma also noted that the legislation to establish a level-playing field between State-owned Enterprises (SOEs) and private businesses was being finalised, with the draft currently under consideration by the Attorney General and expected to be presented to Parliament in the first quarter of 2027.

He said the recent improvement in SOE performance showed that better governance rather than preferential treatment or excessive borrowing could deliver stronger results. “The SOEs are expected to finance parts of their own development programs through improved profitability and reserves, reducing the burden on the Treasury,” he added.

In addition, he said the Budget envisages greater investment in regional airports and connectivity including facilities to enable international visitors arriving at Bandaranaike International Airport (BIA) to connect more conveniently with domestic airports.

The Treasury Secretary also highlighted commercialising the country’s mineral resources via identification, feasibility assessments and international technical partnerships, alongside reforms in agriculture, livestock, irrigation and plantation sector. “A committee has been appointed to review lease extensions and assess companies based on productivity, replanting and land utilisation rather than balance-sheet size alone,” he pointed out.

He said the Government is also seeking to rationalise the tax and regulatory burden on tourism businesses. Responding to long-standing industry concerns regarding overlapping central and provincial-level charges, he said the Government has decided to remove one layer of taxation, with the Treasury providing financial support to the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA).

He also referred to the need to address the financial burden of SriLankan Airlines, which has accumulated losses exceeding Rs. 500 billion since its inception, with a committee appointed to examine the most viable options to minimise the future cost to the Treasury.

Dr. Suriyapperuma reiterated that Budget 2027 was an invitation for businesses to work alongside the Government in translating public investment and policy reforms into sustainable economic goals.

The Forum also featured a panel discussion, comprising Advocata Institute Chairman Murtaza Jafferjee, Standard Chartered Bank Sri Lanka CEO Bingumal Thewarathanthri, who is also Vice Chairman of The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, Small and Medium Enterprise (SME) and export champion Selyn Group of Impact Companies Chief Growth Officer Selyna Peiris, A. Baur and Co Ltd. Managing Director/CEO Rolf Blaser and Treasury Secretary Dr. Suriyapperuma. The panel was moderated by Daily FT Chief Editor/CEO Nisthar Cassim.

The post-Budget Forum’s strategic partner was Standard Chartered Bank; Baurs served as the Gold Sponsor, with Nanaska as Strategic Learning Partner, CICRA as the Technology Partner, Cinnamon Grand as Hospitality Partner and Ogilvy Digital as the Creative Partner.

title: Hayleys makes history: First Sri Lankan listed company to cross $ 1 b in 1H revenue | Daily FT

Hayleys PLC delivered a strong financial performance during the six months ended 30 September, 2026, recording consolidated revenue from continuing operations of Rs. 358 billion, an increase of 33% year-on-year. Profit Before Tax (PBT) rose by 49% to Rs. 21.31 billion, reflecting strong contributions across key sectors.

The Group surpassed $ 1 billion in first half revenue for the first time in its reporting history on the Colombo Stock Exchange, marking a significant milestone in its growth trajectory.

The strong performance was supported by significant contributions from the key export oriented sectors, transportation and logistics and consumer and retail sectors. This performance reflects the strength of Hayleys’ diversified portfolio and its ability to capitalise on opportunities across domestic and international markets.

The domestic operating environment remained broadly resilient, supported by continued economic recovery, although rising inflation and cost pressures presented challenges. Globally, geopolitical uncertainties, commodity price volatility and evolving trade dynamics continued to influence business conditions. Against this backdrop, the Group’s diversified business portfolio, focus on operational efficiencies and strategic investments supported its ability to navigate the evolving operating environment.

Reflecting the Group’s strong operating performance, consolidated EBITDA increased by approximately 46% to Rs. 39.13 billion. Despite an increase in net finance costs, PBT grew by 49% to Rs. 21.31 billion, while profit after tax (PAT) from continuing operations increased by 60% to Rs. 13.63 billion.

During the period, Hayleys PLC was assigned an international ‘B+’ foreign currency rating with a Stable Outlook by S&P Global Ratings. The rating reflects the strengths of Hayleys’ diversified business model and foreign currency earnings base, while providing a globally comparable credit benchmark and supporting access to international capital markets.

Commenting on the Group’s performance, Chairman and Chief Executive, Mohan Pandithage said: “Our strong first-half performance, including the achievement of a historic revenue milestone, reflects the disciplined execution of our strategic priorities and the continued growth of our businesses across domestic and international markets. These results demonstrate our ability to navigate evolving market conditions while capitalising on opportunities across multiple sectors and geographies.”

“As we continue to invest in expanding our capabilities and strengthening our market positions, we remain focused on building a more resilient, competitive and future-ready portfolio. We are confident in the Group’s ability to sustain its growth momentum and create long-term value for our stakeholders.”

Alongside its financial performance, the Group continued to advance its sustainability priorities. Energy intensity declined by 17% year-on-year to 2,902.6 GJ per $ million, while water intensity decreased by 13% to 3,228.0 m³ per $ million. The Group remains committed to achieving a 30% reduction in both energy and water intensity by FY2029/30, against their respective baseline years.

As one of Sri Lanka’s largest private-sector employers, Hayleys continues to support livelihoods and national economic development, employing over 38,200 direct individuals across its operations. The Group’s social impact initiatives in education, livelihoods and community development benefited over 193,330 individuals during the period.

Further reinforcing its position as a leading Sri Lankan corporate, the Group retained its ranking as Sri Lanka’s No. 1 listed company in the LMD 100 for the 11th year.

Looking ahead, while global economic uncertainties and evolving trade conditions remain key considerations, the Group will prioritise operational efficiencies, strengthen profitability and realising greater value from recent investments. These efforts will support continued business performance and the Group’s ability to respond to emerging market opportunities.

The Board of Directors of Hayleys PLC consists of, Chairman and Chief Executive Mohan Pandithage, Co-Chairman Dhammika Perera, Sarath Ganegoda, Rajitha Kariyawasan, Dr. Harsha Cabral, PC, Ruwan Waidyaratne, Jayanthi Dharmasena, Rohan Karr, Gamini Gunaratne, Timothy Speldewinde, Yohan Perera, Jonathan Alles and Rumal Fernando.

title: Sajith brands Budget 2027 a ‘string of lies’ | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:52
-     - 13

Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa

Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa yesterday accused President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake of abandoning Marxism for neo-liberalism. He charged that the 2027 Budget widens inequality, fails to draw foreign investment and offers no relief to farmers, small businesses or public servants.

“This is not a budget; it is a budget of sheer lies,” Premadasa told Parliament in response to the President’s Budget speech on Thursday.

Premadasa said income had shifted from the poor to the rich between 2019 and 2025. Real household income of the poorest 20% fell by 19.6%, while that of the richest 20% rose by 6.8%, he said, widening the average income gap between the two groups from 11.2 times to 14.8 times. He said the richest 20%’s share of income had risen to 55.8%, which he blamed on inadequate wages, soaring inflation and the erosion of living support. He tabled the survey in Hansard.

“The poor were made poorer, and the rich were made richer,” he said.

He said actual foreign investment in 2025 amounted to only $ 1 billion, while projects including the Merchants Logistics Hub, the Petronet Kerawalapitiya project and the Floating Energy Terminal had exited. He questioned how many MAS, Brandix and Hirdaramani factories, pioneers of the 200 garment factories program, had closed in Sri Lanka while those companies opened industrial zones abroad.

“Nothing is coming in; everything is outgoing. Everything is leaving,” Premadasa said.

He said the Government had failed to change the debt sustainability analysis (DSA) agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), as promised in its manifesto “A Thriving Nation – A Beautiful Life”. He said Lazard, the firm that brokered the deal with international sovereign bondholders, had also handled restructurings for Ghana and Senegal, which secured better terms.

He took issue with the macro-linked Bonds in the deal, under which debt relief shrinks as economic growth rises.

“Then what incentive or motivation do we have as a country to increase the economic growth rate? As the growth rate rises, the amount of foreign debt we have to repay also increases. Lazard defrauded Sri Lanka,” he said.

He said there had been no debt restructuring for the 263,000 micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in distress in 2022, a number he said had since grown. The promised development bank for them had not been set up. The Government had suspended the parate law, which lets banks auction pledged property without going to court, but had not restructured MSME debt, he said.

On the digital economy, Premadasa said Rs. 28.5 billion had been allocated, but only five of 17 IT sector promises for 2026 had been delivered. He said the Digital ID promised for the third quarter of 2026 still had no contractor, though one was to be selected by March, and that the IT parks promised in Digana and Nuwara Eliya had not been built.

He said farmers were promised Rs. 150 per kg of paddy, but prices had fallen to a maximum of Rs. 95. He said the promised interest-free loans and price support through small and medium millers had not materialised, and that cultivation of big onions, potatoes, chillies, upland crops, fruit, export crops and upcountry vegetables had collapsed.

“You have not provided even an atom of support for agriculture through this budget,” he said.

Premadasa accused the Government of spending hundreds of billions of rupees of public money on thermal power at the expense of renewable energy, citing the Yugadanavi, Swabhadhanavi and Sahasadhanavi plants, and said the promised LNG had not materialised. He challenged the Government to name a single production industry it had initiated.

He said a World Bank report of October 2026 found that 60% of the country was poor, while the UNDP Multidimensional Poverty Report showed poverty had escalated severely. He said the Government and the Department of Census and Statistics wrongly used a blanket average of 2,030 kilocalories per person per day, when the Medical Research Institute showed needs vary by gender and activity. This error led to the claim that Rs. 17,742 a month was enough for one person, he said.

He said 1.5 million public servants were now treated as a cost by a President who had held them in high regard before the election. Farmers, once called gods and kings, had been branded kasippu (illicit liquor) brewers after the election, he said. He asked why the 15% interest on savings promised to senior citizens had not been granted, and said retirees’ core problems remained unresolved.

Premadasa said the Budget had no proposal for the promised 33% cut in electricity bills, and that pledges of a Rs. 1.2 million Vitz car, a Rs. 50,000 motorcycle and fuel at port landing prices had not been kept.

He said schools could not secure smart boards or computers, and the health sector faced severe shortages of drugs, equipment and staff. He asked what had happened to the promised fish-locating app and the plan to develop marine resources in the 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone. To stem the brain drain, he urged the Government to grant vehicle permits to professionals, including doctors, rather than to MPs.

Recalling the JVP-backed “Saradiel Budget” presented by Sarath Amunugama, which promised to take from the rich and give to the poor, Premadasa said the Government, now holding the presidency, a two-thirds majority in Parliament and most local authorities, had instead presented “a Muhammad Ali budget”. He described it as one that “strikes the stomach of the common man and the poor”.

He urged the Government to reject neo-liberalism and extreme Marxism and adopt “the middle path, social democracy, and the social market economy”.

title: CESS cut on 795 import lines from April 2027 | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:51
-     - 11

CESS will be cut on 795 tariff lines from 1 April 2027 under the 2027 Budget proposals unveiled by President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake on Thursday.

The cuts remove the levy entirely on 499 lines and reduce it by 25% on 64 lines classed as sensitive for local industries, according to lists [issued by: source?].

The larger list, “Intermediate and Capital Goods – List of HS 693”, shows the levy roughly halved on most of its lines as of 1 April 2026. From 1 April 2027, 456 of these lines will become CESS-free. They include paddy and husked rice, crude palm oil, virgin coconut oil, coloured glass and welded steel tubes. Four other lines on the list were already CESS-free as of 1 April 2026.

Another 232 lines on that list will be cut by between about 40% and 50% in April 2027. Maize flour, for example, drops from 13% to 7%, and white cement from Rs. 2 to Rs. 1 per kg. All but one line will be CESS-free from 1 April 2028. The exception is steel T sections, which stay at Rs. 5 per kg in 2027, fall to Rs. 3 per kg in 2028 and reach zero in 2029.

The second list, “Selected Intermediate and Capital Goods sensitive for Local Industries – List of HS 107”, is unchanged until April 2027, when the levy on 64 of its lines will be cut by 25%. CESS on Portland cement in packings of 50 kg and below falls from Rs. 7 to Rs. 5.25 per kg, and on paints from Rs. 150 to Rs. 112.50 per kg. Motorcycle tyres drop from 25% or Rs. 300 per kg to 18.75% or Rs. 225 per kg. Paper packaging, soap wrappers, stationery, polymer dispersions and timber products face similar cuts. Plastic ball point pen barrels keep their 10% rate, but the alternative Rs. 420 per kg rate falls to Rs. 315 per kg.

The levy on 63 of these 64 lines will fall to half its current rate from 1 April 2028. All 64 will be CESS-free from 1 April 2029.

The other 43 lines on the sensitive list will become CESS-free from 1 April 2027 without phasing. They include marble and granite, roofing and wall tiles, squatting pans, steel bridge sections, aluminium doors and windows, sealed batteries, co-axial and other electrical cables, vehicle radiators, silencers and modular steel buildings.

title: Ceylon Chamber says Budget 2027 signals economic transformation, highlights gaps | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:51
-     - 11

The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce yesterday said it encouraged by the broad direction of Budget 2027, noting that it reinforces Sri Lanka’s commitment to economic transformation while maintaining policy continuity, macroeconomic stability, and fiscal discipline. 

“This continuity is particularly important as the country seeks to transition from economic stabilisation to a more durable, investment-led growth trajectory. The Chamber observes that the Budget contains several positive measures aimed at enhancing competitiveness, and external sector resilience, while also presenting opportunities for greater focus on several high-potential sectors that can further accelerate growth,” the Chamber said in a statement.

The Chamber is particularly encouraged by the strong continuity maintained between the 2026 and 2027 Budgets. A number of the key structural reforms identified in last year’s Budget have been carried forward and strengthened, providing greater certainty and predictability to businesses and investors. 

These include the continued implementation of the Trade National Single Window (TNSW), the phased removal of para-tariffs, the rollout of the Digital ID framework, efforts to expand market access through new Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), the strengthening of one-stop-shop investment facilitation mechanisms, progress on Customs reforms, the expansion of Bandaranaike International Airport (BIA), enhanced financing support for SMEs, and reforms relating to the management of State-Owned Enterprises. 

The Chamber also notes with satisfaction that more than 20 proposals submitted by the Chamber have been reflected in Budget 2027. These include measures to strengthen investor facilitation through the establishment of a professionally managed investment promotion agency; continued efforts to improve trade facilitation and export competitiveness; the Government’s consideration of a successor program with the International Monetary Fund (IMF); accelerated progress on key legislative reforms; the expansion of digital Government services; and the promotion of cashless payments and broader digital adoption. 

The Budget has also captured several priorities relating to energy security, including the accelerated deployment of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and investments in fuel storage infrastructure, initiatives to optimise underutilised agricultural land, measures to support the expansion of the digital economy and the IT/BPO sector, and tax reforms to support exporters, including the acceptance of newly VAT-registered exporters as eligible exporters. The inclusion of these priorities reflects the value of sustained public-private dialogue and demonstrates increasing alignment between national policy objectives and the needs of a competitive, export-oriented economy. 

At the same time, the Chamber highlights several areas where the Budget could have placed greater emphasis to strengthen the country’s growth prospects. 

In particular, there is a need for a stronger focus on attracting Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), accelerating factor market reforms, particularly in land and labour, and fast-tracking public procurement reforms to improve the efficiency and speed of project implementation. More targeted and actionable proposals could have been introduced to unlock the potential of sectors with significant growth opportunities, including tourism, agriculture, IT/BPO and logistics.

Overall, the Ceylon Chamber views Budget 2027 as an important step in advancing Sri Lanka’s economic transformation, building on ongoing reforms and incorporating several recommendations advocated by the Chamber. 

The priority now must be effective and timely implementation to translate policy commitments into investment, competitiveness, exports and sustainable growth. The Chamber stands ready to work where possible with the Government and other stakeholders to support the implementation of these initiatives and help move Sri Lanka from economic stabilisation to sustained growth, the Chamber said.

title: JAAF welcomes Budget 2027’s export thrust, calls for swift implementation | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:50
-     - 12

The Joint Apparel Association Forum (JAAF) yesterday welcomed the Budget 2027, which includes a number of the proposals submitted by the JAAF.  

Budget 2027 will strengthen export competitiveness, investment and trade facilitation, JAAF calls for swift and clear implementation so that the benefits reach exporters, workers and investors, it said in a statement.

Apparel remains Sri Lanka’s largest export earner. In 2025, the sector’s exports crossed $ 5 billion, about 32% of total export earnings of $ 17.25 billion. Measures that help exporters compete therefore matter to the wider economy.

JAAF particularly welcomes the following proposals:

Enhanced capital allowance: BOI-approved export-oriented manufacturers investing at least $ 3 million will be able to claim an allowance of 200% of qualifying capital expenditure. This should encourage investment in modernisation, technology and capacity.

Trade facilitation: The National Single Window for Trade will connect exporters in the first half of 2027, supported by an allocation of Rs. 1,990 million. JAAF also welcomes the planned Customs Ordinance reform, the modernisation of the TIEP process and the move towards paperless Customs clearance.

Lower import costs: The 25% reduction in CESS rates across 800 HS code lines is a positive step in the phased reduction of import tariffs.

Support for exporters: Newly VAT-registered exporters will qualify as Eligible Exporters earlier. The Government will also review procedural requirements that can deny legitimate VAT refunds and input tax credits. 

EU partnership: The EU-funded Sri Lanka–European Union Sustainable Trade and Economic Integration Project, worth Rs. 3,430 million over 2027 to 2030, will support export competitiveness and sustainable production.

“Budget 2027 gives exporters a constructive base to build on,” said JAAF Chairman Felix Fernando. “Announcements create confidence, but implementation delivers results. We look forward to working with the Government to ensure these measures are put into practice quickly, so that investors can plan with certainty.”

JAAF looks forward to clarity on several points, in consultation with the Government: Whether the minimum for Enhanced Capital Allowances can be reduced for the SME sector; which HS lines are covered by the CESS reduction, and whether they include raw materials imported for the construction of new manufacturing facilities; clarification on the Indicative Exchange Rate for VAT on Foreign Currency Supplies; the timeline and scope of the National Single Window as it extends to exporters; energy costs and supply stability, which remain critical to manufacturing competitiveness; and, the outcome of the labour law review, in which JAAF hopes to participate through the National Labour Advisory Council.

JAAF also reiterates the importance of continued access to the EU market. The industry supports the Government’s reapplication for GSP+ and will continue to uphold high standards in labour practice, environmental stewardship and good governance. It also remains committed to deepening local sourcing, which strengthens value addition and the resilience of the supply chain.

“The apparel industry employs hundreds of thousands of Sri Lankans and connects the country to the world’s leading brands,” added Fernando. “We are ready to play our part in delivering the growth, investment and jobs this Budget aims for.”

JAAF will continue to engage with policymakers, the private sector and international partners to help build a stable, predictable environment for Sri Lanka’s export industries.

title: Print gets lifeline as Budget 2027 exempts books from VAT, scraps PAL on newsprint | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:49
-     - 10

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake has proposed exempting printed books and exercise books from Value Added Tax (VAT), and removing the 10% Ports and Airports Development Levy (PAL) on newsprint imports from 1 January, 2027. The measures bring relief to students, readers and newspaper publishers.

Presenting the 2027 Budget on Thursday, President Dissanayake proposed the VAT exemption for textbooks, dictionaries, encyclopaedias, children’s drawing and colouring books, educational publications and other printed books, as well as exercise books.

“Printed books and other printed materials became subject to Value Added Tax (VAT) effective from January 2024, while exercise books had been subject to VAT even before that date,” he said.

The President said the exemption recognised the importance of education and the need to keep essential educational materials affordable, with the aim of promoting access to education, knowledge and reading.

The PAL currently charged on the importation of newsprint classified under specified Harmonized System (HS) codes will be removed, he said. HS codes are the international classification used to identify traded goods.

President Dissanayake also proposed a 25% cut in the existing CESS rates on 800 selected HS code lines, under the Government’s program of phased reduction of import tariffs. CESS is a levy on imports. The cut aims to simplify the import tax structure, reduce trade-related costs and enhance the competitiveness of the economy, he said.

title: Modern Pack Lanka wins Gold at CNCI Achiever Awards 2026 | Daily FT

CEO Lahiru Wijerathna (right) and the Modern Pack Lanka team receiving the CNCI Gold Award 2026

Modern Pack Lanka Ltd., has won the prestigious Gold Award in the Extra Large Category at National Level at the CNCI Achiever Awards 2026, organised by the Ceylon National Chamber of Industries (CNCI), Sri Lanka’s oldest industrial chamber. This recognition reflects the company’s commitment to manufacturing excellence, innovation and sustainable growth.

Established in 1993 by Sheamalee Wickramasinghe and Nishka Wickramasinghe as a joint venture with Modern Pack Singapore, the company initially supplied biscuit trays to Ceylon Biscuits Ltd. Over three decades, Modern Pack has grown into one of Sri Lanka’s leading packaging manufacturers, serving customers across the dairy, FMCG, confectionery, bakery, poultry, electronics and apparel sectors.

Its diverse manufacturing capabilities include thermoforming, injection molding, in-mold labelling (iml), blow molding, sheet extrusion and aluminium foil packaging, enabling the company to deliver innovative packaging solutions to leading local and multinational brands.

Modern Pack’s international achievements include winning WorldStar Packaging Awards in 2015 and 2025, presented by the World Packaging Organisation. Recognised as the highest international accolade in packaging, WorldStar celebrates outstanding innovation and excellence. title: Republic and robe | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:10
-     - 14

To rescue the spiritual heritage from political manipulation, the State must look back to move forward. It must re-establish the core tenets of Ashokan Buddhism that Arahat Mahinda brought to the island. Ashokan governance was defined not by giving a monastic monopoly unchecked constitutional vetoes, but by active State purification of the Sangha, enforcing strict moral accountability. These make-believe edifices built on elite preservation and structural immunity are historically unsustainable

Anuradhapura, the enduring crucible witness to grand history of our noble kings, has today turned into an amphitheater for a comic opera staged by a disparate and desperate opposition. 

In a frantic bid for survival, a strange coalition of the Rajapaksa’s Ranil Wickremesinghe, Sajith Premadasa, and Dilith Jayaweera have all lined up to present themselves as the new champions of the saffron robe.

Of all the opposition mandarins, Sajith Premadasa stands out as the most eloquent reservoir of hogwash, vehemently insisting that no secular law can ever supersede the inviolability of the saffron robe. 

He completely forgets that the Enlightened Master explicitly directed his followers to stitch their robes out of ‘paansa kula’ the discarded, decaying cloths gathered from cemetery cadavers.

They all rush to the Ancient City to launch their bids to return to relevance and credibility! Yet, the street-level agitations of the saffron-clad political actor known as Balangoda Kassapa was never a spontaneous movement. 

It is nothing but a theatrical curtain-raiser for a much broader, systemic offensive against the NPP Government and President Anura Kumara Dissanayake (AKD).  It is a war by other means—the other means being the saffron shield.

The true scale, scope, and purpose of the saffron iceberg broke cover with a staggering institutional directive. In a letter dated 30 October 2026, the Mahanayake of the Kotte Chapter of the Siam Maha Nikaya, Most Ven. Dr. Ittapana Dhammalankara Thera, officially requested the Commissioner General of Prisons to arrange a date and time for a ten-member delegation of the Sangha Sabha to enter Welikada Prison to conduct a formal re-robing ceremony for the convicted monk Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara. 

By demanding that a secular prison, with its rigorous order, be pliant enough to bend to ecclesiastical jurisdiction under their interpretation of what the Buddha taught as Dhamma and what the Buddha dictated as ‘Vinaya’, the Kotte Chapter of the Siam Nikaya hierarchy has brought the nation-State to a critical crossroad. 

Are we a modern republic?

We are compelled to ask a foundational question that fifty years of constitutional appeasement of the Sangha Order have sought to evade—first in the 1972 constitution, and second with the 1978 constitution. 

Are we a modern, true Republic in the Rousseauvian sense—where the General Will of sovereign citizens is absolute—or are we a de facto theocracy where judicial accountability stops at the command of the Buddhist supra clergy. 

In his ‘The Social Contract’  Rousseau leaves no room for such ecclesiastical dualism. He dictates that sovereignty is nothing less than the exercise of the General Will, declaring that it is ‘inalienable’ and that ‘the sovereign, who is no other than a collective being, can be represented only by himself.

To Rousseau, any private faction or partial society that demands a separate exemption from the common law breaks the social pact, for the collective citizenry alone holds the absolute authority to govern the republic.

The foundational architecture of this self-inflicted crisis was laid during the post-independence era.

Buddhism and Constitution

To understand how a convicted prisoner can have an entire monastic council march into a State facility to restore his institutional armor, one must trace a self-inflicted crisis built on constitutional appeasement and absolute neo-liberal mischief. Let us not forget that Gnanasara performed his first contemptuous dance against the judiciary inside the Homagama Magistrate’s Court, wrapped in that very same saffron robe. Now, the Kotte Kalyanasri Sangha Sabha intends to stage another epic farce inside the walls of a secular State prison.

The structural decay began under the 1972 Constitution, introduced by the Sirimavo Bandaranaike-led United Front Government.

In a bid to appease a majoritarian Buddhist psyche, the 1972 constitution granted Buddhism the ‘foremost place’ and mandated the State to ‘protect and foster’ it.

This piece of constitutional mechanics legally transformed the monastic hierarchy from spiritual guides into constitutional stakeholders holding an implicit veto over State policy.

This historical trap was aggressively expanded in 1978 by that Latin-epigram-loving political fox, J.R. Jayewardene (JRJ).While fondly quoting ‘Infelix qui sancta docet si vivat inique’—’Unfortunate is the one who teaches holy things but lives wickedly’—JRJ executed a maneuver of profound neo-liberal mischief.”

JRJ expanded the constitutional mandate to include the preservation of the nebulous ‘Buddha Sasana’.  By institutionalising the ‘Sasana’ a term elastic enough to encompass not just spiritual sublime doctrine, but vast networks of untaxed monastic wealth, extensive land ownership, and autonomous temporalities such as the Dalada Maligawa, Sri Padasthana, and Atamasthana—the State created a parallel, unregulated, but venerated quasi-State.

The subsequent creation of a dedicated Buddha Sasana Ministry effectively insulated the clergy from secular auditing and legal oversight, rendering the hierarchy structurally immune to the rule of law.

We would do well to remember that even the Kandyan King Keerthi Sri Rajasinha, who facilitated the historic 1753 return of the higher ordination from Siam, fiercely retained absolute sovereign authority over the clergy.

Not only did he reserve the right to appoint the Sangharaja, but when a palace assassination plot was uncovered in 1755, he promptly imprisoned the newly appointed Sangharaja Welivita Sri Saranankara ‘Therunwahanse’ on suspicion of complicity.

If an 18th-century absolute monarch understood that spiritual robes do not grant immunity against the laws of State survival, why has a modern democratic republic forgotten it? President AKD, it is time to learn from our history.

The current standoff exposes the ultimate irony of our contemporary political landscape. A disgruntled political class, having lost their grip on the nation’s rudder, is now reduced to the sorry state of clinging to the aging udder of a worn-out sacred cow. When retired Admiral Sarath Weerasekara—a blinkered ideologue of the old guard and now media mogul DJ’s fellow 

traveller—is seen holding backroom meetings at five-star hotels with Kasun Kularatne alias Balangoda Kassapa under the guise of paying homage, the farce is laid bare.

Surely, the Buddha Sasana Ministry should possess the precise details of Balangoda Kassapa’s  registration, the recognised Nikaya to which he belongs, and the specific ecclesiastical lineage from which he received his higher ordination! 

That it does not is the ultimate proof of an intentionally constructed blind spot in this whole business.  

The old regime can no longer rely on the traditional Sangha hierarchy, which has occasionally shown institutional restraint.

Instead, they are forced to subsidise, amplify, and weaponise independent actors masquerading in saffron to manufacture moral panics on demand. 

They are aided by private television channels brazenly dedicated to giving them unhindered, unlimited exposure under the convenient cover of freedom of expression.

Whither saffron robe?

Under free-market global commerce, the essence of Prince Siddhartha’s renunciation has been distorted into a corporate shield by an entrepreneurial priestly class.

By simply draping a piece of cloth over his shoulders, any political agitator can instantly inherit a shield of constitutional immunity that protects them from secular State auditing, penal codes, and judicial mandates.

Has anyone ever bothered to ask some of these saffron-garbed potentates why they sport an additional, glistening saffron shawl thrown so stylishly over their shoulders? 

To some, the saffron robe has ceased to be a symbol of world-renunciation. It has become a fashion statement and a marker of elite status. 

This sorry state completely exposes the modern myth of the Arahat Dhajaya—a faith marketer’s coinage designed to stress the absolute sacred status of the robe-wearer. In the cultural imagination of the island, the saffron robe is revered as the very pennant of Arahat Mahinda, son of Ashoka, who according to legend brought the Dhamma to the rock of Mihintale.

Yet, according to eminent historian Romila Thapar, Arahat Mahinda’s visit to Mihintale was not a miraculous, vacuum-born conversion of an ignorant king. 

Rather, his objective was institutional organisation. Mahinda arrived as an official envoy of a highly sophisticated Mauryan State to formalise religious ties, organise monastic orders, establish a disciplined monastic code (Vinaya), and structurally align the Anuradhapura monarchy with the State-patronised Buddhist models of Emperor Ashoka. The deeper details of that structural discussion could await another day. 

The saffron robe was meant to signify the ultimate conquest of ego, greed, and worldly power.

But when the robe is used to protect individuals from criminal investigations, evade court orders, and host political strategy sessions with discredited politicians, it ceases to be the pennant of Mahinda.

It becomes a cynical costume of political convenience, degrading the very heritage it claims to protect.

That said, the opposition’s calculations fail to account for the organic, unyielding dynamics of the Aragalaya. The 2022 uprising was fundamentally a post-nationalist awakening that shattered the old ruling elite’s ability to trigger automatic communal, religious, and tribal reflexes. The consecutive electoral triumphs of the NPP completely disrupted a cozy ecosystem that had survived for seventy-six years.

Duplicitous devotion

The modern Sri Lankan citizenry has learned a brutal economic lesson. They now know that a politician’s duplicitous devotion at a temple does not prevent the bankruptcy of a nation. 

The organic consciousness of the Aragalaya acts as a discerning firewall against these manufactured crises, rendering the old guard’s tools obsolete.

The entire Buddhist monastic establishment is now forced to make a defining choice between 21st-century modernity or tribal primitivism. 

Will the Maha Sangha evolve into an exemplary spiritual body bound by moral accountability, or will it persist as an unregulated parallel Government clinging to feudal land ownership, untaxed wealth, and medieval legal immunities? 

If President AKD and the NPP Government are genuinely committed to a systemic overhaul, they must confront this historical trap head-on. The State must completely repeal the British-inspired Buddhist Temporalities Ordinance, cutting monastic property management off from the State’s benevolent Nelsonian eye.”

To rescue the spiritual heritage from political manipulation, the State must look back to move forward. It must re-establish the core tenets of Ashokan Buddhism that Arahat Mahinda brought to the island. 

Ashokan governance was defined not by giving a monastic monopoly unchecked constitutional vetoes, but by active State purification of the Sangha, enforcing strict moral accountability.

These make-believe edifices built on elite preservation and structural immunity are historically unsustainable.

The Welikada prison re-robing theater and the Anuradhapura Satyagraha are not revivals. They are the final, desperate gasps of a feudal-minded oligarchy both lay and ordained resorting to the oldest trick in the book.

title: From monsoon to management: Colombo’s heavy weather and building a flood-resilient Sri Lanka – Part I | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:05
-     - 19

The problem therefore requires a change of philosophy. Sri Lanka must move from flood control to integrated flood-risk management. The distinction is significant. Flood control seeks to keep water out or move it away. Flood-risk management accepts that extreme rainfall will occur and seeks to ensure that the landscape, infrastructure, institutions and population can absorb its consequences without catastrophic damage

Colombo’s recent inundation is not adequately explained by exceptionally heavy rainfall alone. It is the consequence of an increasingly dangerous convergence of meteorological extremes, urban development, degraded natural drainage, infrastructure limitations, institutional fragmentation and human behaviour.

The immediate trigger was an extraordinary burst of rainfall on 6 November. The underlying vulnerability, however, has been accumulating for decades.

On 7 November, Colombo Municipal Council (CMC) officials reported approximately 129 mm of rain in one hour, against a drainage system design capacity of approximately 30 mm per hour.

The Meteorological Department separately attributed the event to intense thunderstorms associated with the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) and second inter-monsoon conditions. It also identified obstructed drains as an aggravating factor.

This distinction is fundamental. Meteorology supplied the extraordinary volume and intensity of water. Urban development reduced the terrain’s ability to absorb and retain it. Inadequate drainage and maintenance prevented its timely removal. Institutional and social shortcomings increased the consequences.

It was a perfect storm – except it was worse than imperfect for hundreds of thousands of inundated householders, stranded motorists, sundry soggy pedestrians et al.

The policy implications are manifold. Sri Lanka cannot prevent extreme rainfall; nor can it engineer its way to complete immunity from flooding. It can, however, substantially reduce flood frequency in vulnerable locations, limit flood depths and duration, protect lives and livelihoods, and reduce the economic cost of disasters.

The recommended approach is a national program of integrated flood-risk management, combining engineering, ecological restoration, land-use reform, institutional accountability, meteorological intelligence and community preparedness.

The meteorological dimension

So why did Colombo receive so much rain?

Firstly, there are the immediate atmospheric conditions. This early November event occurred during Sri Lanka’s second inter-monsoon season, which normally unfurls over the island in October–November.

The country’s rainfall calendar is not governed by one continuous monsoon. It comprises four principal seasons:

The first inter-monsoon (March-April) has localised thunderstorms and convection as its principal characters. This is followed by the south-west monsoon, with heavy rainfall in western and southwestern areas.

The second inter-monsoon is what you and I are wading through at present. That is followed by the north-east monsoon (December-February), with rainfall particularly in the northern and eastern regions. It often affects the central areas too, of late, as does the south-west monsoon before it.

Three atmospheric processes are relevant to the recent inundation.

Firstly, the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), which is a broad belt of low pressure where winds from the Northern and Southern Hemispheres converge. This convergence encourages warm, moist air to rise. As it rises, it cools and condenses, producing clouds and thunderstorms.

During the second inter-monsoon, the ITCZ migrates across Sri Lanka. Its presence, combined with favourable atmospheric instability, can produce exceptionally intense rainfall.

Secondly, convective thunderstorms, where unlike prolonged monsoonal rainfall, convective storms can discharge enormous quantities of water over relatively small geographical areas and short periods.

This is particularly dangerous in Colombo. A drainage system might cope with 100 mm of rain distributed over 24 hours, but fail catastrophically when a comparable proportion falls in under one hour. The 6 November event demonstrated precisely this catastrophic vulnerability.

Thirdly, atmospheric oscillations and oceanic influences, in addition to which two additional phenomena deserve attention. The Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO), a large-scale eastward-moving atmospheric disturbance with a cycle of approximately 30-60 days, which influences tropical cloud formation and rainfall. And the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) that influence rainfall variability over longer periods.

Research published in the Journal of Climate in 2023 identifies particularly strong MJO-related influences on Sri Lankan rainfall during the second inter-monsoon and southwest monsoon seasons. Research also identifies associations between MJO phases and extreme precipitation events.

These phenomena help explain why rainfall can become unusually intense during particular periods. However, without a detailed meteorological attribution study, it would be premature to identify a particular MJO, ENSO or IOD configuration as the cause of the 6 November storm.

Is climate change responsible?

Climate change is an important part of the larger picture, but we should distinguish between two propositions: a) that climate change is increasing the risks associated with extreme rainfall; and b) that climate change caused this particular rainfall event. The first is scientifically well-founded. The second requires event-specific attribution research.

A warmer atmosphere can hold approximately 7% more water vapour for every 1°C increase in temperature, under the relevant thermodynamic approximation. This can increase the potential intensity of rainfall when atmospheric conditions produce precipitation.

Other relevant factors include: changes in monsoon circulation; variations in the frequency and intensity of thunderstorms; changes in the distribution of rainfall between seasons; rising sea levels, which can impede the discharge of inland stormwater; and greater exposure of urban settlements to extreme weather.

A recent World Bank assessment identified Greater Colombo as particularly vulnerable because of its concentration of people, economic assets and infrastructure. It also documented the expansion of flood-exposed built-up areas.

The policy conclusion is that Sri Lanka should design infrastructure for future rainfall conditions, rather than relying exclusively on historical rainfall averages.

The cultural-historical dimension

There is an interesting cultural and philosophical dimension to Sri Lanka’s relationship with rain.

The Pali expression “devo vassatu kalena, sassasampatti hotu” is best translated: ‘May rain fall in due season; may the harvest be plentiful.’

This traditional Buddhist blessing expresses a relationship between rainfall, agricultural prosperity, social wellbeing and the natural order.

It is particularly meaningful in a country whose civilisation developed around agriculture and sophisticated water management.

But there is an important distinction between rain in due season and destructive rainfall.

The blessing is not an endorsement of unlimited precipitation. Its underlying aspiration is for rainfall that is timely, sufficient and conducive to life.

Sri Lanka’s ancient hydraulic civilisation provides a particularly instructive counterpoint to contemporary urban flooding.

The tank-and-reservoir system developed over centuries was based on capturing, retaining, regulating and distributing water.

The cascade systems of the Dry Zone connected small tanks, larger reservoirs, streams and agricultural land into interconnected hydrological networks.

The principle was not simply to dispose of excess water. It was to retain water where it could be used, while allowing controlled movement through the landscape.

The ancient principle commonly expressed as ‘wewai dagabai gamai pansalai’ captures the relationship between the water tank, temple, village and community.

There is a lesson here for modern urban planning. Colombo’s wetlands, marshes, canals and retention areas are not vacant land awaiting development. They are part of a living water-management system.

The cultural contradiction

There is a contradiction between Sri Lanka’s historical reverence for water and some contemporary practices such as filling wetlands to create commercial and residential property, building on natural drainage paths, dumping household and commercial waste into canals, treating marshes as wasteland, and regarding flood protection as the responsibility of Government rather than a shared civic obligation.

It would be simplistic to blame these practices on a decline in cultural values alone. They also reflect economic incentives, land scarcity, planning failures, poverty and inadequate enforcement.

Nevertheless, the cultural dimension matters. A sustainable flood policy requires a change in the way society understands wetlands and waterways: from obstacles to development into essential public infrastructure. And a closer inquiry into why Sri Lanka has suffered repeated flooding.

A historical perspective

Flooding is not a new phenomenon in Sri Lanka. It is a recurring feature of the country’s geography, climate and settlement patterns.

The important question is why a country with such a long history of water management continues to experience devastating floods.

The historical record illustrates the persistence and geographical breadth of the problem:

The record reveals two important things: first, flooding is a national problem, not merely a Colombo problem; second, the nature of the risk varies substantially according to location.

Water, water everywhere!

There are five principal categories of flooding:

Firstly, riverine flooding occurs when rivers overflow their banks following prolonged or exceptionally heavy rainfall in their catchments. Major vulnerable river systems include Kelani Ganga, Kalu Ganga, Gin Ganga, Nilwala Ganga, Mahaweli Ganga and Attanagalu Oya.

The Kelani basin is particularly important because of its proximity to Colombo and its exposure to rainfall in the central highlands. Heavy rainfall upstream can produce flooding downstream, even when Colombo itself has experienced relatively little rain.

Secondly, urban flash flooding: this is the most relevant category for the recent Colombo event. Rain falls faster than the drainage network can absorb and discharge it. Water accumulates on roads, in low-lying residential areas and around commercial buildings. The principal problem is often a combination of inadequate drainage capacity, insufficient storage and obstructions.

Thirdly, reservoir-related flooding. Reservoirs are essential to Sri Lanka’s irrigation and electricity systems. However, high inflows, reservoir operating constraints and releases can contribute to downstream flooding. This requires coordinated water management, particularly where several reservoirs and hydropower facilities affect the same river basin.

Fourthly, coastal and estuarine flooding. High tides, storm surges, sea-level rise and sediment accumulation near river mouths can impede the discharge of inland water. This is especially relevant to Colombo, where drainage outlets ultimately depend on the hydraulic conditions of the Kelani River and the Indian Ocean.

Fifthly, landslides and secondary disasters. Flooding and landslides frequently occur together. Heavy rainfall in the central highlands can cause slope failures, damage roads, interrupt communications and isolate communities. The 2016 and 2017 disasters demonstrated how one meteorological episode can produce multiple interconnected emergencies.

Oh, Colombo!

Why is Colombo so particularly vulnerable? The city occupies a low-lying coastal basin. Its historical landscape included extensive marshes, paddy fields, wetlands, lakes and interconnected waterways.

These features performed an essential hydrological function. They absorbed rainfall, temporarily stored excess water and allowed its gradual discharge into rivers and the sea. Urbanisation has progressively compromised this system.

One of the most consequential developments has been the reduction of natural flood-retention areas. Wetlands function as natural reservoirs. They slow runoff, retain water and release it gradually. The World Bank has highlighted that Colombo’s wetlands can store several million cubic metres of water during periods of intensive rainfall.

Its assessment of the city’s wetland system also demonstrated that drainage tunnels and pumping stations alone cannot adequately protect Colombo if its natural retention areas are lost.

A 2025 University of Moratuwa study examining Colombo’s land-use changes between 1999 and 2022 found that urban expansion and the reduction of green spaces and natural retention areas increased surface runoff and flood vulnerability.

Then there is all of this unplanned urban development whereby buildings, roads, car parks and paved surfaces prevent rainwater from infiltrating the soil. Consequently, rainfall that would previously have been absorbed by vegetation and marshland becomes surface runoff.

The cumulative consequences are substantial. More water enters drainage channels, water reaches canals more quickly, peak flows become higher, existing drains become overloaded, flooding occurs even in locations that previously experienced little inundation.

The World Bank’s assessment of Greater Colombo records a significant expansion of flood-exposed built-up areas.

A key factor is inadequate drainage infrastructure. The reported disparity between the recent rainfall intensity and the drainage system’s design capacity is particularly revealing…

Reported rainfall intensity versus drainage design capacity is instructive. Reported rainfall on 6 November was 129 mm/hour. Reported drainage design capacity is 30 mm/hour. Therefore the approximate ratio of reported rainfall intensity to reported drainage design capacity was x4.3.

The problem is not simply that Colombo needs larger drains. It needs a drainage system designed as an integrated network – with adequate storage, unobstructed canals, functioning gates, appropriate pumping facilities and sufficient discharge capacity.

Several recurring problems have been identified in technical studies: waste accumulation in canals and drains; unauthorised construction obstructing waterways; commercial development within wetland reservations; inadequate maintenance of drainage channels; insufficient storage capacity; restricted outfalls and backwater effects.

A particularly important technical consideration is that Colombo’s drainage network is connected to the Kelani River and the sea. High river levels or tides can restrict the discharge of stormwater. In certain circumstances, a drainage outlet that normally carries water away may become ineffective.

A study of Colombo's flood-adaptation options identifies inadequate outfall capacity, insufficient storage and reduced canal conveyance as three central problems.

Institutional fragmentation is perhaps the most important governance issue. For example, the Land Development Corporation is responsible for major drainage channels, while the Municipal Council has responsibility for much of the local drainage network.

Nor is Colombo’s drainage system managed by one institution: different responsibilities are distributed among the Colombo Municipal Council, Sri Lanka Land Development Corporation, Urban Development Authority, Road Development Authority, Irrigation Department and other local authorities and public agencies.

The World Bank has specifically identified the division of responsibilities between these institutions.  The danger is that a problem at one point in the system can undermine the performance of the entire network. A municipality may clear its drains, for example, but if a downstream canal is obstructed, the benefit may be limited.

The sociopolitical dimension

Flood vulnerability is also a consequence of the way land, development and public resources are governed. Several issues deserve attention.

Firstly, there is unequal enforcement. Unauthorised structures can obstruct canals and waterways. But enforcement must apply consistently to residential encroachments, commercial developments and politically connected property interests. It would be unfair and ineffective to place the entire responsibility on low-income communities living in flood-prone locations.

Secondly, there are development incentives whereby land reclamation and construction can generate immediate private economic returns while transferring the cost of increased flood risk to the wider public. This is a classic case of externalised environmental costs.

A third is political short-termism: drainage maintenance, wetland conservation and flood-resilience investments rarely produce the immediate political visibility of roads, buildings and other construction projects. The result can be an imbalance between investment in development and investment in the systems that make development sustainable.

A fourth is institutional discontinuity: flood mitigation is a long-term undertaking. Changes in political leadership, administrative priorities and public sector budgets can interrupt projects that require continuity over decades.

A fifth is inadequate accountability: after major floods, investigations, emergency meetings and declarations of new programs are common. The more important test is whether the findings lead to measurable improvements in infrastructure, enforcement and maintenance.

The creation of a special Colombo flood-response task force was announced by the Presidential Secretariat on 7 November 2026. This is a potentially useful immediate response, but its effectiveness will depend on whether it develops into a properly resourced, accountable institutional arrangement.

The central policy problem

Sri Lanka has treated flooding as an emergency rather than a permanent development challenge. Our resilient island nation has repeatedly demonstrated that it can mobilise resources after a flood. The harder task is to prevent the underlying conditions from recurring.

There is already considerable technical knowledge available. The Metro Colombo Urban Development Project, initiated in 2012, included improvements to drainage, canals, retention areas and urban infrastructure. The Sri Lanka Land Development Corporation also undertook substantial hydrological and hydraulic modelling.

These initiatives established important foundations. But the recurrence of serious flooding suggests that engineering interventions have not been sufficient to eliminate systemic vulnerabilities.

The problem therefore requires a change of philosophy. Sri Lanka must move from flood control to integrated flood-risk management. The distinction is significant. Flood control seeks to keep water out or move it away.

Flood-risk management accepts that extreme rainfall will occur and seeks to ensure that the landscape, infrastructure, institutions and population can absorb its consequences without catastrophic damage. This is the foundation of the policy framework being proposed in this article.
