(The author is the Editor-at-large of LMD and is a senior journalist with a Post-graduate Diploma in Politics and Governance)

title: Sri Lanka’s foreign policy paradoxes: Geo-politics, development and human rights | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:00
-     - 20

Former Foreign Secretary Ambassador Ravinatha Aryasinha

Former Foreign Secretary Ambassador Ravinatha Aryasinha has said the 21st Century paradoxes Sri Lanka’s foreign policy faces—regional geo-politics, economic development and human rights accountability—cannot be resolved simply by responding individually to satisfying the competing ‘zero-sum’ demands made by major powers, but required addressing the underlying weaknesses that have made Sri Lanka vulnerable to such external pressures in the first place. 

He said, “Our strategic location should be an asset, not a source of perpetual uncertainty; our economic relationships should generate opportunities for sustainable growth, rather than deepen existing vulnerabilities; and our engagement with the international organisations should be guided by a consistent commitment to international law, rather than playing along ambiguously. This calls for a foreign policy that is informed by a broader national consensus, supported by effective institutional safeguards, and implemented through a professional diplomatic service”.

Amb. Aryasinha, who is presently the Executive Director of the Regional Centre for Strategic Studies (RCSS), made these observations when he delivered the 2026 ‘Gamani Corea Memorial Lecture’ on the theme The Paradoxes of Sri Lanka’s Foreign Policy in the 21st Century on 4 November 2026 at the BCIS in Colombo, amidst a representative gathering comprising serving and retired public figures, diplomats, entrepreneurs, academics, civil society, media and students.

Opening the event, Gamani Corea Foundation (GCF) Chairman Dr. Harsha Athurupana said the memorial lecture honoured Dr. Gamani Corea, the distinguished Sri Lankan economist and former Secretary General of UNCTAD, and noted that the GCF supports scholarly research through grants, collaborates with Universities and Institutions Dr. Corea was connected to, and also the ‘Freeda Corea Awards’  - named after his mother, supports disadvantaged women who are engaged in initiatives that enriched their communities. The speaker was introduced by GCF Board of Management Member Manjula de Silva.

Amb. Aryasinha commencing the lecture, said “Dr. Corea’s contribution to international economic diplomacy was rooted in the conviction that developing countries, including smaller states, need not simply accept the terms of an international order shaped by others. Through the strength of his ideas, his diplomatic engagement and his work in institutions such as UNCTAD and the South Centre, he helped give collective expression to the concerns of developing countries and advance the case for a more equitable international economic system.”

In his address, Amb. Aryasinha observed that Sri Lanka’s foreign policy ever since independence was replete with paradoxes, but they were consciously faced head-on, straddled with, and to a considerable extent overcome. Despite Prime Minister D.S. Senanayaka in 1947 signing Defence and Foreign Affairs agreements with the British, UNP administrations resisted western colonialism, opposed war reparations on Japan, and went on to sign the Sino-Lanka Rubber Rice Pact. Prime Minister Sirimavo Bandaranaike a founding leader of the NAM in 1961, also demonstrated scrupulous objectivity between the West and the East. President J.R. Jayewardene though adopting the western neo-liberal economic model in 1977, nevertheless proclaimed that “non-alignment runs like a golden thread through the fabric of our country’s foreign policy”.

In juxtaposition, he said 21st Century Sri Lanka foreign policy, particularly post-2009, has lacked conceptual clarity, with contrasting ‘foreign policy postures’ adopted by alternate political administrations, with paradoxes often leading to crisis.

Regional geo-politics

He said the first paradox with respect to regional geo-politics, was that Sri Lanka’s location is both its greatest asset and its greatest risk – the more the major powers value it, the less room Sri Lanka has to choose freely. Resisting the “Zero-sum” environment Sri Lanka had been placed in, proved to be the ‘crucial test’ to Sri Lanka’s foreign policy making. Notwithstanding the material losses and emotional strain that had to be endured by the Sri Lankan polity, the IMF Extended Fund Facility (EFF) of 2022/23, provided a positive disruption in arresting this trend, albeit temporarily, as all competing powers had to come together, allowing Sri Lanka foreign policy - from ‘pendulum swinging’ to return to the centre. Sri Lanka presently stands at a crossroads, with the “strategic space” nearing its end in March 2027 and GOSL’s call whether to continue with the IMF, and if so, under what terms - no doubt a complex economic issue which requires close study, also has profound foreign policy implications. He said he sensed that the jostling for position has already begun, and that any who encourage that Sri Lanka returns to behaviour tantamount to bandwagoning with one single power - who ever that may be, are doing a grave disservice not only to Sri Lanka, but also to their preferred country, others who are over-looked, and also to a host of traditional friends, middle powers and regional blocks.

Economic development

The Second paradox he drew attention to was Sri Lanka’s long standing quest for economic development - thwarted initially by the 30 year separatist conflict, and in the immediate post-conflict period had a more competitive environment prevailed Sri Lanka may well have avoided some of the strategic mistakes and other difficulties it was to face in subsequent years. Today, while acknowledging the resilience the economy has shown amidst severe internal and external shocks—from Ditwah to the on-going war in the Middle East, and despite the anti-corruption emphasis and lessening of the diplomatic temperature - global markets are not opening up to Sri Lanka and international investors are not knocking on our door as expected. He said, structural barriers make the Sri Lankan economy uncompetitive, and it has also failed to increase export revenue, diversify its export basket and export markets adequately. According to the recent EBD Report of the first 3 quarters of 2026, while exports to India and China are up - 12% and 16% respectively, exports to our largest single market - the United States remained flat, and shipments to the UK have dropped by over 9%. While much hope had been placed on the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) to which Sri Lanka’s application for membership is pending since 2023, the region’s share in Sri Lanka’s trade, services and investment portfolio remained low. He said Sri Lanka’s Western partners could also help trade, investment and tourism flows by improving the ‘OECD Risk Rating’ on Sri Lanka which since 2021 remains at 7 - the highest possible, and also through more favourable travel advisories.

Human rights

 The third paradox of concern was human rights accountability, where getting the balance right in protecting human rights, while fighting terrorism/violent extremism has been a challenge in modern times. He noted that while Sri Lanka had adopted postures of compromise, collaboration, and confrontation in the past, currently the paradox lies in the fact that the posture adopted in the HRC by Sri Lanka since 2024 can at best be described as one of ambiguity - opposing the Sri Lanka Accountability Project (SLAP) in its statements in the HRC, but being unwilling to challenge it and permitting it to be passed unopposed. Additionally, in parallel asking the HRC to do away with the ‘Çountry Specific Mandate’ targeting Sri Lanka, while the High Commissioner for Human Rights (HCHR) insists that an international mechanism is vital for confidence building of the victims, but unwilling to share the OHCHR findings. Whether the driving factor in this is Norms, Laws, or Power Politics is hotly contested the world over - and clearly evidenced in Sri Lanka, with many - including most victims on all sides, seeing it as the latter.

Amb. Aryasinha, who served as Sri Lanka’s Permanent Representative to the UN (2012-2018), noted that once placed on the HRC agenda, there was no transparent objective criteria for moving out of it, which remains a serious lacuna in contemporary human rights governance. This suggests that often being allowed to move from a confrontational to a conciliatory path has largely been for collateral purposes, rather than due to any genuine improvements perceived or achieved in country’s human rights record. If one is serious in seeking sustainable approaches to addressing human rights issues in the HRC, he said it would be reasonable to demand a realistic ‘sufficiency threshold of delivery’, as opposed to the current imprecise and changing demands being made by the multitude of external actors.

Ambassador Aryasinha said straddling and overcoming these paradoxes, calls for a foreign policy that is informed by a broader national consensus, supported by effective institutional safeguards, and implemented through a professional diplomatic service capable of anticipating developments rather than merely reacting to them. It also requires us to look beyond the immediate calculations of major-power relations, to cultivate partnerships with middle powers and regional groupings, and to make fuller use of multilateral institutions in advancing issues of common interest. Above all, Sri Lanka must recover the capacity to articulate what it seeks from the world, and to pursue those objectives with consistency, credibility and purpose. It is in this respect that the example of Dr. Gamani Corea remains so relevant.

title: Building economy our grandchildren can depend on | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:00
-     - 13

We plan future debt repayments and strive to grow earnings from established sources. But can these alone secure our future? We must also open entirely new income pathways today, so that future generations can reap the benefits

Imagine a little girl preparing to enter school in January 2027, excited about her new uniform, books and the world opening before her. She knows nothing about international borrowing, debt restructuring or the foreign currency obligations Sri Lanka will face as she grows up. She did not choose those obligations. Yet the decisions we make today will influence the opportunities available to her and, one day, to children not yet born.

In our village gardens stand magnificent old fruit trees planted by grandparents and great-grandparents. Some of those who planted them never lived to enjoy their full harvest. We still gather the fruit and enjoy the shade, often without thinking about the people whose foresight made this possible. They planted for generations they might never meet. What are we planting today for ours?

Sri Lanka has made important progress in recovering from the economic crisis of 2022. The efforts to restore stability, restructure debt and rebuild confidence deserve recognition. But recovery and long-term economic security are different achievements. The first deals with the crisis we have experienced; the second asks whether we are building an economy less vulnerable to the next one. It demands that we think not only of this year or the next Budget, but of 2035, 2040 and beyond.

The danger is real, even if it is not always visible in daily life. The IMF’s May 2026 assessment projects foreign currency public debt service averaging about 3.3% of GDP annually over 2027 to 2032. That is a substantial call on the country’s future external resources, alongside the foreign exchange needed for imports and other international payments. Borrowing can be productive and necessary, but recurring dependence on new external financing, without expanding our capacity to earn, leaves future generations exposed. The child entering school next year will live with the consequences long after today’s decisions have passed from public memory.

Our Treasury rightly devotes serious attention to fiscal management, debt sustainability and future repayment schedules. Yet an improved Budget balance in rupees does not, by itself, ensure access to the dollars needed for external obligations. That requires a strong and resilient capacity to earn from the world, together with prudent external financing and reserves. The Treasury’s Medium-Term Debt Management Strategy for 2026 to 2030 shows the value of planning ahead. Should we not complement that discipline with a similarly purposeful plan for creating additional earning capacity?

Increasing exports, tourism, established services and other existing sources of income remains essential. Much professional effort already goes into improving their performance, productivity and access to markets. But there is a second task, distinct from doing more of what we already do: identifying and making possible entirely new kinds of business activity. Better results from existing channels do not automatically create new channels. Unless we deliberately open them, they may never feature in our future earnings.

Harvest may take years, opening channels need not

A fruit tree takes years to mature, but planting it need not. A new industry may likewise take years to develop products, earn the trust of customers and produce substantial recurring income. In many cases, however, the enabling step is much quicker: clarify a regulation, remove an avoidable restriction, introduce a workable procedure or secure a coordinated decision. Some proposals will require legislation or substantial safeguards, and those must be respected. But the natural time required for a business to grow should never be confused with the time needed to make its establishment possible.

As an industrialist who has spent decades developing products and entering international markets, I have found that entrepreneurs rarely lack the motivation to seek customers or take commercial risks. Often, their most valuable help from Government is not another promotional program, but a predictable, competitive environment in which they are free to act. An entrepreneur may already have a supplier, an overseas customer, financing and a sound business model, yet be unable to proceed because existing arrangements do not permit the transaction. Finding that entrepreneur another customer will not solve the problem. What is needed is an environment in which the business can start and grow. 

Think of the old irrigation canals. Water and fertile land may both be available, but crops cannot grow until the channel reaches the field. Government’s essential role is to open such channels through lawful, practical facilitation. Entrepreneurs can then invest, compete and create the harvest. A well-designed framework can serve many enterprises, not just a single applicant, and may give rise to commercial opportunities that no official plan could have predicted.

The establishment of ViYASA, the National Business Facilitation Centre (NBFC), under the Presidential Secretariat is therefore a welcome development. Its work in overcoming regulatory and administrative obstacles provides an opportunity to go beyond solving problems faced by existing businesses. With a clear mandate and effective coordination, it could also enable new earning and foreign exchange saving activities that are not yet practical under present arrangements.

There are surely more opportunities than any one institution can identify on its own. A few proposals for new pathways are understood to have reached ViYASA already, and many more could come from businesses, professional bodies, universities and industry associations. The important step is to give promising, viable ideas a dependable route from submission to a decision and, where justified, to an operational framework. Until that happens, even an excellent proposal remains only an idea.

Practical commitment to future generations

Budget 2027 offers a timely opportunity to make this commitment and begin the practical work that must follow. The Treasury and Presidential Secretariat could commit to a ten-year program for developing additional net foreign exchange earning and saving capacity, complementing existing debt and economic planning. ViYASA could coordinate the practical activation of an initial group of commercially credible pathways, each with one accountable lead, the specific obstacle identified and a target date for a decision. An initial 30-day action program could focus on securing decisions for pathways ready to proceed, while placing more complex legal or regulatory matters on clearly defined timelines.

The program need not attempt to forecast the precise earnings of every new venture. Instead, a simple quarterly report could record three things: how many new pathways have become legally and operationally available, how many businesses have begun using them, and what genuinely additional net foreign exchange they have earned or saved. The last measure must account for associated foreign currency costs and distinguish realised results from projections. Such reporting would connect present facilitation with the earnings that may emerge over the following five or ten years.

A brief commitment in the forthcoming Budget would be a valuable beginning, even if the full program is developed during 2027. It would not require Government to choose every business, find its customers or finance its investments. It would establish something more enduring: a responsibility to keep opening productive opportunities and to show, quarter by quarter, what has become possible. The question at each review would be simple: what new earning activity can Sri Lankans undertake today that they could not undertake three months ago?

Our grandchildren will inherit more than the financial obligations of our generation. They will inherit the opportunities we create, or fail to create, while we have the chance. Those still unborn had no voice in the borrowing decisions of today; surely they deserve our foresight in building tomorrow’s earning capacity. We cannot promise them a future without risk or debt. We can, however, work to leave them an economy less dependent on borrowing to meet its needs, and better able to prosper through what it produces and earns.

Our grandparents planted trees without knowing who would gather the fruit. We continue to enjoy their gift. Let us respond with the same quiet sense of duty: open the channels now, enable new activities to take root, and allow time for them to flourish. The harvest may take years, but the planting must be done now.

(The author is a Chartered Engineer, Founder and Chairman of the KIK Group of Companies, an export-oriented engineering and switchgear manufacturer and a Presidential Export Award winner. The views expressed are his own. He can be reached at lalith@kik.lk)

title: Enduring resistance | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:00
-     - 18

Grappling with the profound shifts in the global order seems especially foolhardy these days. But occasionally, it is also uplifting exercise when it seems we are on the cusp of change that, however tentatively, may produce a better order out of the hegemonic one that is crumbling.

The US midterm elections—right on the heels of Lula’s crushing of the far-right candidate, Flavio Bolsonaro, in Brazil—proved to be a real shock. The US results appear to be as decisive as Trump’s initial victory in 2016, when he won the upper Midwest that has long been associated with post-industrial decay.

In the case of the most recent electoral results, the inroads of the Democratic Party into the South anticipate a potential transformation. That includes the possibility that the Democratic party line affiliation becomes competitive again in the region, only this time organised along the lines of multiracial democracy.

It appears to be the end of the generational loss of the South to the Democratic Party, which Lyndon Baines Johnson feared would be the outcome of the Voting Rights Act. That Act was the legislative capstone of the Civil Rights Movement. Its dismantling by the Supreme Court in the Louisiana v. Callais case this year is what shaped the political earthquake of the midterm elections.

While keeping this poetic reversal in mind, there is also a brute reality we must face: as much as ‘vibes’ have arguably taken over elections in many places around the world, in places like the US there is still a material contradiction at the core of the AI boom that has yet to be resolved. The economy continues to diverge between the fortunes of capital and labour. However, there is no guarantee that the diverse constituencies marshalled under opposition to Trump will cohere into a durable bloc.

Still, the mere fact that they voted in a way that subverted the hackneyed claim of irreversible polarisation gives us a clue as to how things might become unstuck and start moving again in terms of the great confrontation with wealth and power. This struggle is essential for avoiding the most disastrous outcomes for the planet. The spectre of destruction became especially visible this year with the unhinged joint US/Israeli assault on Iran as part of the broadening of Israel’s sanguinary campaign in Gaza and beyond, and last year with the Trump trade shock.

Changing external orientation

Meanwhile, what might the US posture be towards the rest of the world because of the tremendous churn in the country’s politics? It is not obvious if, and even how, it might try to revive its hegemonic position. Deploying the 1960s ‘Cold Warrior’ as the closest analogy, New York Times columnist Jamelle Bouie argued that in his victory speech, Jon Ossoff, the victorious Democratic senator from Georgia, embraced rhetoric very close to the ‘evil empire’. Only in this case, Ossoff used it to describe MAGA fascism, not the Soviet Union.

As a domestic metaphor, it was a deft counterpoint to the right-wing attempt to turn the US midterm elections into another Red Scare, which was laced with noxious Islamophobia for good measure. But in terms of foreign policy, the explanatory power of this analogy is limited by the fact that the US battle against domestic totalitarianism cannot be projected as part of a reassertion of its global hegemony, which continues to unravel.

There is no Vietnam that sits on the other side of the Civil Rights Movement. In fact, Democrats along with most of the country already rightly resist Trump’s reasons for the war against Iran. Some of the core myths of American hegemony have been perhaps permanently shattered by imminent strategic defeat in the Gulf. That includes the potential emergence of a new security order—perhaps order is too strong a word, given the highly transactional nature of the repressive regimes involved—based on mutual non-aggression between countries like Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Iran.

Of course, Israel remains the wild card given the paroxysm of violence it has unleashed. In his piece, “The Collapse of Zionism”, Israeli historian Ilan Pappe observed the parallel with the dying apartheid regime in South Africa.

At the same time, there is Russia. It remains a gravitational lens for the West’s political anxieties—in the past conservative, today progressive, with the latter’s fears surrounding the global expansion of the far right. Even in the age of Marx, he considered the Tsardom the ‘gendarme of European reaction’. Strategically though, Russia’s aggressive expansionism is a non-starter as the rationale for renewed US ambition, given that the European Union sees the absolute need, at least rhetorically, for a separate defence umbrella.

The transatlantic relationship has permanently ruptured under Trump. That does not mean that the US and the EU will no longer collaborate as part of a residual hegemony that they exercise on a contingent basis in other parts of the world. But the relationship is no longer an unquestionable pillar of support for the US’s global ambitions.

Meanwhile, China has served as a convenient bipartisan adversary. It has taken the place of the Soviet Union in reflecting both tremendous technological potential and a supposed enemy that must be contained. But military confrontation in the Pacific remains perhaps even less likely. The demonstration effect is powerful in what the US and Russia have encountered while trying to subdue far weaker countries in the age of drone and missile defence.

While Xi Jinping has concentrated an enormous amount of power around himself—not to mention the fact that sabre rattling is always useful for distracting from economic malaise—unless he reaches Trumpian levels of delusion, China will likely continue to apply pressure in ways that do not necessarily lead to decisive confrontation in the Taiwan Strait. Still, the US has long inserted itself into regional politics. It is unclear if and how there would be a return to détente in the region, especially with the growth of militarism and the increasing insertion of Big Tech into the US national security State.

A Nascent anti-imperialism?

This looming question is where US domestic politics will almost certainly play a role in determining the unravelling of its imperial trajectory. Democrats may discover a purpose not only in regulating frontier AI development because of its impact on local communities, but also the corollary that by confronting tech overlords, they must reckon with a major shift in attitude towards the exercise of military power abroad.

Already Elon Musk’s gamble to throttle Starlink in Ukraine has produced murmurs about the need for nationalisation. And Musk’s role in the assault of the ‘Department of Government Efficiency’ on federal bureaucracy is almost certain to come under powerful congressional scrutiny. However, war making is not only the arena of private tech oligarchs. It is also the animating principle of the modern State.

Perhaps even more relevant, it remains extremely unclear whether there is genuine space for anti-imperialism, given that the US’s financial fortunes have been tied to the maintenance of its global hegemony.

Already Trump has crowed that the reversal in stock market gains in the aftermath of Democratic victory is the result of the threatened overturning of his AI agenda. If finance is heavily intertwined with the fortunes of a decent segment of the American electorate, then it is unclear what other kind of settlement would produce an electoral bloc that can resist the tendency to conflate fiduciary responsibility for people’s retirement portfolios with all the aggressive entrapments of what world systems scholar Peter Gowan called the ‘Dollar-Wall Street Regime’.

This argument does not mean we must revert to the assumption that the ‘labour aristocracy’ in the West is constitutively incapable of producing material alliances with working people in the global South. But it is a fact of politics that the organisation and maintenance of class hegemony in the US through finance has inserted a time bomb into the social order.

It must be defused carefully to avoid provoking the kind of resentment and frustration that could support revanchist moves to try and claim as much plunder abroad to compensate for further downward mobility among the ill-defined ‘middle class’. Trump’s gambit might have temporarily failed in Iran. But unless it is replaced by a clear alternative, the most extreme elements of aggression abroad could reappear.

The global south

Nevertheless, with the US midterm results, there is a renewed possibility of a political challenge to finance on a world scale. The interest rate shock initiated by US Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker in the late 1970s was the death knell for proposals for a New International Economic Order. It plunged developing countries into severe debt crisis as debt servicing costs skyrocketed in the 1980s. But the new Democratic affordability agenda raises broader questions about what kind of finance is possible under alternative, more progressive circumstances.

It would be extremely ironic if neoliberalism, having claimed to slay the inflationary dragon in the West, is in turn unmade by underinvestment in sectors like renewable energy, which could have eased the pain of post-Covid supply shocks. This is to say nothing of what would happen if there was another financial crisis and attempted bailout of banks or other powerful actors that reeks of corruption. The latter already became an explicit target of public anger and frustration in the US midterm elections.

At the same time, the potential reversal of the class project of finance capital may not provide immediate relief to peripheral countries that are on the frontlines of climate change and debt crisis, even while facing IMF-mandated austerity. As others have pointed out, the latter has restrained the investments needed to cope with shocks. But growing scrutiny of Big Tech, and, by extension, finance within the metropole could create breathing room for countries in the global South to at least conduct more of their own domestic experiments. In this case, the results of the US midterm elections are yet another data point revealing a possible progressive turn in the global order, even if they are not the ultimate result.

At the very least though, we should be aware of how our shared global terrain is being reshaped. Latin American historian Greg Grandin has pointed out in his lyrical history ‘America, América’ that North and South are interlinked in their destinies. Much as Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s New Deal helped facilitate Import Substitution Industrialisation in Latin America under figures like Getúlio Vargas, and vice versa, we may be at another historical juncture.

For example, the structural changes that occurred in the global order during and after the Great Depression—especially the wide acceptance of capital controls—facilitated the domestic experiments needed for countries to either rebalance their economies or begin the long process of development in the aftermath of the tremendous colonial extraction that occurred. On the other hand, the current AI boom also represents perhaps the most extreme form of what the political economist Robert Brenner has called the ‘politically driven upward redistribution of wealth’.

There is plenty to fear about the potential tendency towards dispossession. Sri Lanka was threatened with it only several years ago at the height of its economic crisis, including the attempted fire sale of its assets. But the US midterm elections and Lula’s victory in Brazil also show that there are always going to be forces of resistance. More than the national boundaries that supposedly resemble coherent geopolitical blocs, it is the ongoing ‘civil war’, as Lenin reminds us, that will be central to restraining finance capital and the imperial powers backing it.

In the context of recent political developments abroad, even a small country like Sri Lanka may find more room for manoeuvre to engage in experiments that were long since banished as anathema to the market. That includes revitalising the public sector without fear of the kind of foreign policy crisis that temporarily resulted in the suspending of US aid in the early 1960s, when Sri Lanka nationalised its oil industry. In this regard, geopolitics is intimately tied to economic relations.

But equally important are the ideological imaginaries shared across places, which can inspire solidarity. New political frameworks are being hammered out in an ongoing battle across an extremely fragmented global landscape, despite tremendous dangers, whether war, fascism, or worse. As the recent elections in the American antipodes show, this struggle has far from been determined. That elusive moment when the tide looks like it may turn offers hope amid chaos.

title: Why we must treat atmosphere as global common | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:00
-     - 12

The same right that allows the mining of the commons of air for private profit must recognise the right to replacement, where privately produced gasses are placed into the commons of air. In this way the Global Commons of Air could act very much as a global bank to hold and account for the critical stocks it accepts into and dispenses out of the global capital

There is an urgent need to consider our responsibility by the most ubequitious and essential common resource, air! The atmosphere has been identified as a Global Common by every national and internaional statement to date. The Global Commons are the Earth’s shared natural resources and environmental domains that lie outside the political jurisdiction of any single nation-state.  The assumption being that, because no individual country owns them, all nations share access to and responsibility for them.

International law traditionally recognises four core domains as Global Commons.

1. High Seas: The open ocean areas beyond national exclusive economic zones (more than 200 nautical miles from a coast).

2. Atmosphere: The layer of gases surrounding the planet that regulates climate and air quality.

3. Antarctica: The southernmost continent, governed by the Antarctic Treaty System

4. Outer Space: The void beyond Earth’s atmosphere, including celestial bodies and orbits

It is the commons of air or the atmosphere of Earth that requires urgent address. The atmosphere, is the multi-layered mixture of gasses that surround Earth’s planetary surface which is retained by gravity.  It is comprised of 78 percent · Nitrogen, 21 percent Oxygen ,· 0.93 percent Argon and 0.04 percent Carbon dioxide . Although Oxygen is the third most abundant element in the universe, Free molecular Oxygen or (O2) is one of the rarest things in the entire universe. The only place known to have it is the atmosphere of planet Earth. This phenomenon began when the earliest plants began colonising the land about 470 Ma  adding Oxygen to the atmosphere.  Again continued onwards until by 400 Ma, when present levels atmospheric oxygen was reached. At these levels fire became a planetary feature which then helped to maintain the subsequent evolution of the atmosphere.

Currently, the free Oxygen in the atmosphere is about 1.2x1015 tonnes (12,000,000,000,000,000 t), but it is unstable in our planet’s atmosphere and must be constantly replenished by photosynthesis of green plants.  Recent human activity, mostly the burning of fossil fuels and deforestation have led to an increase in the concentration of Carbon Dioxide and a decrease in Oxygen.

Not just gasses

In addition to gasses, Earth’s atmosphere also contains variable quantities of suspended aerosols and particulates that can effect human health and create weather features such as clouds and hazes. Particulates or fine particulate matter with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers or less, which is about 30 times smaller in diameter than a human hair, is known as PM 2.5. Because of its tiny size, it stays in the air for a long time and can travel deep into the lungs and bloodstream.

Another significant pollutant of the atmosphere are the Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs). These are carbon-based chemicals that easily turn into gas and evaporate into the air at room temperature. When VOCs react with sunlight and nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere, they form ground-level ozone and are a primary driver of photochemical smog and atmospheric haze. Chronic or high-level exposure can cause permanent damage to the liver, kidneys, and central nervous system. Certain common VOCs, such as benzene, formaldehyde, and methylene chloride, are known or suspected carcinogens linked to cancer.

A recently detected substance of concern that affect air quality are the Microplastics, defined as, “synthetic solid particulate matter or polymeric matrices, with regular or irregular shape and with size ranging from 1 μm to 5 mm, of either primary or secondary manufacturing origin, which are insoluble in water”. They represent the final stage of erosion of these resistant chemicals within the environment that they are released into.  There is now an airborne fraction of microplastics consisting of synthetic polymer particles smaller than 5 mm (often less than 1 mm, structured as fibers or fragments) suspended or transported in the atmosphere. These small microplastic particles can remain in the atmosphere for up to one year, facilitating their transport around the globe. They have now become cloud condensation nuceli (CCN) intensifying rainfall in many areas.

Recent research  by scientists at the Stockholm University reveals that rainwater across every region of Earth is now contaminated not only with microplastics but also now contains toxic per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) at levels  that exceed safety limits set by major health agencies.

Much like plastics they are known as ‘forever chemicals’ due to their extreme resistance to natural degradation, these man made compounds have circulated through the global water cycle, contaminating even the most pristine and isolated regions, including Antarctica and the Tibetan Plateau. This pattern of widespread dispersal means that rainfall everywhere on the planet is no longer safe to consume without specialised purification.

These chemicals have been manufactured for decades in products like nonstick cookware, waterproof gear, and firefighting foams, leaching into waterways and cycling into the atmosphere via ocean spray. Exposure to such persistent pollutants is linked to severe long-term health risks, including various forms of cancer, compromised immune systems, decreased fertility, and developmental delays in children.

But we have to remember it’s not just the microplastics or just PFAS, that have began to degrade the quality of the air we breathe; it includes pharmaceuticals, herbicides, pesticides adsorbed onto PFAS, plastic and partially combusted carbon. The quality of the very air we breathe is being eroded.  The warning has been given by the loss of flying insects and invertebrates that use the air as their living enviroment, as the quality of air goes down so do the creatures who live in it. This is why 70% to 80% of all flying insects in agricultural fields are gone and why biodiversity is declining at a rate of 1% year on year.

The commons of air have largely become a repository to the ‘negative externalities’ produced by industrial and transport activities of the modern economic system. These negative externalities are exemplified by the process of obtaining energy for industry or transport. All the combustion gasses of burning fossil carbon compounds, provoke a cost to the environment but that cost is considered a ‘negative externality’ and the person discharging these toxins has no responsibility nor cost for that action.

This assumption implies, that if a process produces a benefit to the environment during its activity, it must be considered a ‘positive extenality’ and reflect a value for that action. If the product is something that is being taken out or mined out of the commons, the replacement of what has been lost must have value. The same right that allows the mining of the commons of air for private profit must recognise the right to replacement, where privately produced gasses are placed into the commons of air. In this way the Global Commons of Air could act very much as a global bank to hold and account for the critical stocks it accepts into and dispenses out of the global capital.

title: Assassination of Kavantissa: Coincidence, negligence, or an ideological message? | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:00
-     - 65

Kavantissa

The title poses a difficult and uncomfortable question. Before dismissing it, however, it is worth examining the remarkable chain of events that followed the alleged shooting of Kavantissa in late September. Failures appear to have occurred, or been permitted to occur, at every stage, from the incident itself through to Kavantissa›s burial and its aftermath. Such widespread failures rarely stem from a simple error of judgement by one individual or the shortcomings of a single institution. More often, they point to something deeper and more serious. This article explores those possibilities, but first we must establish the facts. 

The facts

Kavantissa, the legendary tusker from Galgamuwa, believed to be about 45 years old, died on 16 October 2026 after his health deteriorated over several weeks following a reported shooting in September. Many wildlife conservationists, enthusiasts, animal lovers, and others reportedly kept the authorities regularly informed of Kavantissa›s condition through various channels. Many accounts point to what appears to have been a striking lack of engagement by the authorities responsible for Kavantissa›s welfare. Given the animal’s iconic status, critics, such as Dr Ajantha Perera and Tissa Jananayake, publicly argue that the response of the Department of Wildlife Conservation and other officials fell far short of what the situation warranted. 

On 31 October 2026, a Sri Lankan television channel broadcasted a report alleging serious misconduct and a shocking lack of professionalism on the part of wildlife veterinarians responsible for treating Kavantissa. According to another credible media report published in early November, the tusker had reportedly been allowed to go missing for approximately six days during treatment in early October, causing critical delays in the administration of essential follow-on medication, although the accuracy of this report has not yet been conclusively established. Meanwhile, according to another media report, an interim post-mortem report submitted to the court on 11 November revealed that three bullets had been found in Kavantissa›s abdomen region. 

The controversy did not end with Kavantissa›s death. Reports alleged that the animal’s body was severed at the neck into two parts and buried separately within hours, in a manner that many regarded as undignified and deeply disrespectful to one of Sri Lanka›s most celebrated tuskers. The handling of the remains sent shockwaves throughout the country and compounded the grief and outrage felt by thousands of people. We saw grown men and women crying in public. 

Throughout the entire saga, the apparent indifference displayed by senior Government leaders, including the President, was particularly striking. Despite widespread public concern, there appeared to be little acknowledgement of responsibility, little expression of remorse, and little urgency in addressing the growing criticism surrounding the case. Yet, within days of Kavantissa›s death, the Government announced a new initiative aimed at safeguarding all elephants and ensuring their proper treatment across Sri Lanka. 

The Questions

Given the extraordinarily high public profile of this tusker, and the fact that many private individuals had offered to make funding available for Kavantissa›s treatment, many people have questioned why the authorities did not promptly devote more resources to his care. If the wildlife authorities had sought additional resources, there were individuals willing to provide them. If they had requested expertise, there were individuals ready to offer it. And if they had sought international expertise, there were individuals willing and able to fund the engagement of specialists from overseas.

The alleged shooting was a failure of wildlife protection. The untimely death was a failure of wildlife treatment. The undignified burial was a failure of compassion and remorse. Together, these events have left thousands of grieving Sri Lankans asking one simple question: Why was Kavantissa, an innocent animal with no known history of attacking humans, treated in this manner? Was this merely a failure of an individual or an institution, or does it point to something more sinister that every Sri Lankan should be concerned about?

The Communist Ideology 

Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP), the dominant force within the NPP coalition Government, is rooted in a political tradition heavily influenced by communist ideology. Communist ideology is broad, but one of its central principles is the pursuit of greater social and economic equality, and at its core lies a deep suspicion of privilege, hierarchy, and special treatment. While the pursuit of equality is a noble objective, problems emerge when equality is interpreted so rigidly that excellence, distinction, and achievement are viewed as undesirable or even threatening. 

Traditionally, Sri Lankan society has been almost the opposite of this strict interpretation of equality. We celebrate and reward fellow Sri Lankans who distinguish themselves through beauty, intellect, musical talent, acting ability, public speaking, writing, or sporting achievement. As a result of their talents and accomplishments, such individuals often acquire greater wealth, influence, or recognition. In Sri Lankan society, as in most non-communist societies, such outcomes have generally been regarded as legitimate rewards for merit and effort. In contrast, some interpretations of communist ideology view the emergence of exceptional individuals and the concentration of status or wealth as obstacles to a more equal society because they create visible social distinctions and hierarchies. 

An ideological message?

When senior NPP-JVP figures declare, “we have the Government, but not the State,” they are revealing more than they intend, and far more than many Sri Lankans realise. The significance of that statement deserves a detailed discussion of its own, but we do not have space to discuss the meaning of this statement in detail here. In essence, however, it suggests that while political power has been secured through electoral victory, the broader project of transforming the nation›s institutions, values, culture of governance, and ultimately its constitutional order strictly along communist lines remains incomplete. In that context, Kavantissa was more than a tusker, but an ideologically uncomfortable, symbolically profound obstacle. 

Kavantissa was a distinguished tusker, celebrated for his size, stature, temperament, and grandeur. He was a symbol of distinction, prestige, and public admiration. To an ideology uncomfortable with distinction, prestige, and status such a symbol can become an obstacle, not much as a physical obstacle, but as a powerful psychological one. When an ideology seeks to reshape a society, it does not stop with changing institutions. It seeks to redefine what people admire, respect, and aspire to become. 

This raises a troubling question: Was the handling of Kavantissa›s case, culminating in his death and followed almost immediately by an initiative to protect all elephants, intended to send an ideologically charged message rooted in communist thinking that the NPP-JVP Government would grant special treatment to no one, regardless of merit, circumstance, and public sentiment, even when the consequence is the loss of a valuable life? 

Are you, as a Sri Lankan, prepared to be a victim of such an ideology? Today it may be Kavantissa. Tomorrow, could it be you?

(The author, an Engineering Professor born, bred, and educated in Sri Lanka, a graduate from the Faculty of Engineering at the University of Peradeniya with First Class Honours, can be reached via: dushyantha.basnayaka@gmail.com)

title: Rain- and bad-light-hit Test ends in draw | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 14 November 2026 00:31
-     - 6

Saud Shakeel missed out on a century for the second time in the match

Milan Rathnayaka helped himself to three Pakistani wickets in the second innings

RAWALPINDI: With more than 120 overs lost over the five days, a draw was the only realistic result possible in the first cricket Test between Sri Lanka and Pakistan at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium, here yesterday.

The biggest talking point was Saud Shakeel missing out on another century in the match. Out for 93 in the first innings, Shakeel who played remarkably well in the second innings to ensure that Pakistan drew the Test was unlucky for the second time when he was bowled by Lahiru Kumara for 97. He had not scored a Test century for two years and came twice close to doing so.  

Sri Lankan bowlers started off well yesterday by striking off the first ball, but the partnership of 92 between Saud Shakeel and Ghazi Ghori for the seventh wicket, brought Pakistan back into the game. Shakeel held one end together with a gritty knock that lasted 210 balls and included seven fours. Ghori contributed 35 off 69 balls.

The partnership sealed the fate of the Test. Shakeel and Ghori began positively after lunch but gradually slipped into a more cautious approach, rotating the strike and seeing off Sri Lanka’s bowlers without taking unnecessary risks. Milan Rathnayake once again managed to conjure something out of nothing, getting Ghori to glove one behind to the keeper. Shakeel continued to hold one end together, in the company of Arafat Minhas who fell off the final ball of the session.

Saud Shakeel cops a blow on the shoulder during his defiant innings of 97

The morning began in dramatic fashion as both overnight batters, Azan Awais and Mohammad Taha, were dismissed within the first five deliveries. Sri Lanka exploited the conditions brilliantly throughout the extended morning session and captured four Pakistani wickets.

Babar Azam walked in with positive intent and struck a few boundaries. He was handed a reprieve when Kamindu Mendis dropped him on 22, but the Pakistan Captain failed to make Sri Lanka pay, departing for 34. Sri Lanka also came up with some unconventional field settings and reaped the rewards, with Babar and Salman Agha falling to those plans. Shakeel and Ghazi copped a few blows as the pitch continued to spice up, but they continued to bat solidly.

There were positives for both teams: the four debutants acquitted themselves pretty well for Pakistan with Saqib Khan getting a 7-fer in his debut and taking the Player of the Match award while for Sri Lanka their middle-order batted with authority, as did their pace bowlers. Kusal Mendis on his debut as Test Captain distinguished himself with a century and seven catches in the match. He had good company with Dhananjaya de Silva who went on to make a big hundred, which was instrumental in Sri Lanka’s revival.

The second Test will start on 17 November and will be played at the same venue following Lahore’s inability to host the match due to fog issues.

Sri Lanka swiped Scotland by four wickets to secure their second successive win in the ICC Women’s Emerging Nations Trophy match played at Karwan SC cricket grounds, Ajman yesterday.

Sri Lanka were once again lucky with the toss and having invited Scotland bat first kept them under a score of 111-8 with some exceptional bowling from seamer Sathya Sandeepani (2/18) and left-arm spinner Sugandika Kumari (2/15).

Scotland’s prolific opening batter Darcey Carter displayed her prowess by making a top score of 62 off 55 balls (3 fours).

So tight were the lines and lengths maintained by the Lankan bowlers that they conceded only five boundaries in the entire Scotland innings.

Sri Lanka‘s run chase was controlled by opening batter Vishmi Gunaratne who once again showed fine form to get her team across 

the line. She missed out on back to back fifties when she was dismissed for 49 with Sri Lanka needing three runs for victory. Vishmi who took the Player of the Match award struck 3 fours and 1 six in her 41-ball knock.

Sri Lanka faltered in the middle overs losing three wickets for 6 runs, mainly to leg-spinner Abtaha Maqsood (3/18), but Vishmi’s steadying influence saw them home with 11 balls to spare.

With two wins in as many matches Sri Lanka are virtually through to the Super Six. They head Group A with 4 points and have two more games against Papua New Guinea on Sunday and UAE on Monday to complete their first round fixtures.
